slides.say: Square K L M N is circumscribed about a circle, and square P Q R S is inscribed in the circle. What is the ratio of the area of P Q R S to the area of K L M N?
at: Square K L M N is circumscribed

slides.say: Circumscribed means the big square is around the circle, and the circle touches its sides. Inscribed means the small square is inside the circle, with its corners on the circle. So they ask for the small square's area over the big square's area.
at: So they ask for the small

slides.say: [short pause] It's an inscribed and circumscribed question again. We'll solve it by plugging in numbers, and then by understanding, with symmetry.

Let's check one thing first. The corners of P Q R S are on the circle, but the question doesn't say where. We can turn the small square inside the circle. Its corners stay on the circle, so its size doesn't change. So let's turn it until its corners are at the points where the circle touches the big square, as in the figure.

[short pause] No length is given. If we make this whole figure bigger, every length grows by the same factor. So both areas grow by the same factor, and their ratio stays the same. So we don't need letters. Like in the last question, we pick an easy radius, one.
Look at the big square's side, L M. It's as long as the diameter of the circle, because the circle touches both sides. So the side is two, and the area is two times two, four.
at: Look at the big square's side
the area is two times two

slides.say: Now the small square. A lot of students go through silver triangles. In the corner at K there's a silver triangle with legs of one and one. So its hypotenuse, the small square's side, is root two. Squaring it, the area is two.

There's another way too, with the whole small square. A square's area is also diagonal times diagonal, over two. The diagonals of P Q R S are diameters of the circle, two each. Two times two, over two, is two.
So the small square over the big one is two over four, a half. None of the choices has r in it, so we just look for a half. Choice number two is our answer.
at: Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's solve it by understanding, with symmetry. We use the turned position again, with the corners of P Q R S at the touching points. Draw the diagonals of the small square, P R and Q S. They cut the big square into four small squares.
at: Now let's solve it by understanding

slides.say: Look at the small square in the corner at K. The side P Q is its diagonal, so it cuts it into two identical triangles. One is inside P Q R S, and one is outside.
It's the same in every corner. So the big square is made of eight identical triangles, and P Q R S is made of four of them.
Four out of eight is a half. So the big square is twice the small one, and the answer is a half. Choice number two again. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
